question: Which two fields are required on every `LLMTestCase`, regardless of which metric you plan to run?
options: A) input and actual_output
B) input and expected_output
C) actual_output and retrieval_context
D) context and retrieval_context
explanation: input (the user query) and actual_output (your app's real response) are the only two mandatory fields on LLMTestCase -- every other field (expected_output, context, retrieval_context, tools_called, expected_tools, token_cost, completion_time) is optional and only required by specific metrics. B is wrong because expected_output is optional, only needed by metrics like Contextual Precision/Recall or answer-quality GEval checks. C is wrong because retrieval_context is optional and only needed by RAG metrics. D is wrong because neither context nor retrieval_context is universally required -- context feeds Hallucination, retrieval_context feeds Faithfulness/Answer Relevancy/Contextual*, and a test case with neither is still valid for e.g. GEval on input/actual_output alone.

question: You're debugging why FaithfulnessMetric scores are misleading. Someone points out you should not confuse `context` with `retrieval_context`. What's the actual distinction?
options: A) They are aliases for the same field; deepeval accepts either name
B) context is the static, ideal ground-truth chunks from your dataset; retrieval_context is what your retriever actually returned at runtime
C) context is used only for multi-turn tests; retrieval_context only for single-turn
D) context is required by all metrics; retrieval_context is deprecated in favor of context
explanation: context is your dataset's static, curated ground truth -- the ideal chunks that should exist regardless of retriever behavior -- and it feeds referenceless-ground-truth metrics like HallucinationMetric. retrieval_context is what your retriever actually pulled back at runtime for that specific query, and it feeds Faithfulness/Answer Relevancy/Contextual Precision/Recall/Relevancy. Comparing the two lets you isolate retriever quality from generator quality. A is wrong -- they're distinct fields with different semantics, not aliases. C is wrong -- both apply to single-turn LLMTestCase; the multi-turn analog uses per-Turn retrieval_context. D is wrong -- retrieval_context is very much active and is required by the majority of RAG metrics.

question: In a ConversationalTestCase built from a list of Turn objects, when are retrieval_context and tools_called valid fields on a Turn?
options: A) Only when role="user", since users trigger retrieval
B) Only when role="assistant", since only the assistant retrieves context or calls tools
C) On every turn regardless of role
D) Only on the first turn of the conversation
explanation: A Turn's retrieval_context and tools_called are only meaningful on assistant turns, since it's the assistant (your system) that performs retrieval or invokes tools in response to the user -- a user Turn is just role="user" plus content. Setting these on a user turn is a no-op / schema violation in deepeval's model. A is backwards -- users ask, they don't retrieve. C is wrong because setting them on user turns has no semantic meaning and deepeval scopes them to assistant turns only. D is wrong -- there's no special-casing of the first turn; the role-based rule applies uniformly across the whole conversation.

question: You build an ArenaTestCase with two Contestants to compare GPT-4 vs Claude-4 on the same question using ArenaGEval. What will deepeval do if the two contestants' `input` fields don't match exactly?
options: A) It silently uses the first contestant's input for both
B) It throws an error -- all contestants' input (and expected_output, if given) must match exactly
C) It averages the two inputs into a merged prompt
D) It runs two independent evaluations instead of a head-to-head comparison
explanation: ArenaTestCase exists specifically for head-to-head comparison of contestants answering the *same* input, so deepeval enforces that all contestants' input fields (and expected_output, if any contestant sets it) match exactly -- otherwise you're not comparing apples to apples, and it raises an error rather than silently proceeding. A and C are wrong because deepeval never silently mutates or merges your data -- it fails loudly on a mismatch. D is wrong because that defeats the entire purpose of Arena mode, which is relative (winner-picking) scoring via compare(), not absolute per-contestant scoring.

question: ArenaGEval is run via `compare(test_cases=[...], metric=arena_geval)`. Why does deepeval auto-mask contestant names and randomize their order before sending them to the judge LLM?
options: A) To reduce token usage during judging
B) To remove judge bias -- LLM judges can otherwise favor a model by name or by consistent positional ordering (e.g. always picking the first option)
C) Because model names contain PII that must be redacted
D) It's required by the OpenAI API terms of service
explanation: LLM-as-judge evaluators are known to exhibit both name bias (favoring a model they 'recognize' as strong, e.g. GPT-4 by name) and position bias (systematically preferring whichever answer appears first/last in the prompt). ArenaGEval mitigates both by anonymizing contestant identity and shuffling presentation order before the judge sees them, so the winner is picked on merit, not on branding or ordering artifacts. A is wrong -- masking/randomizing doesn't meaningfully change token count. C is wrong -- model names like 'GPT-4' aren't PII. D is fabricated; there's no such ToS requirement.

question: Comparing the three test case types, which statement correctly describes component-level (@observe-based) evaluation support?
options: A) All three (LLMTestCase, ConversationalTestCase, ArenaTestCase) support component-level eval
B) Only LLMTestCase supports component-level eval; multi-turn is conversation-level only and Arena doesn't apply the concept
C) Only ConversationalTestCase supports component-level eval, since conversations have multiple turns to instrument
D) Only ArenaTestCase supports it, since comparing contestants requires per-component breakdown
explanation: Single-turn LLMTestCase is the unit that @observe-based tracing attaches metrics to at the span level, so it fully supports component-level evaluation. ConversationalTestCase has no component-level concept -- multi-turn evaluation is conversation-level only, scored via evaluate() after simulation, with no tracing support. ArenaTestCase is n/a for this axis entirely since it's about relative comparison via compare(), not span-by-span scoring. B correctly captures this three-way split; A, C, and D each misstate which type(s) actually support it.

question: You want to debug a single failing metric on one test case as fast as possible, with no reporting or caching needed. Which run method is the right fit?
options: A) evaluate(test_cases=[tc], metrics=[m])
B) assert_test(tc, [m]) inside a pytest function
C) metric.measure(test_case)
D) deepeval test run test_file.py --official
explanation: metric.measure(test_case) is the direct, standalone call meant exactly for this: debugging a single metric against a single test case, with the score and reason immediately available on the metric object. It skips evaluate()/deepeval test run entirely, which means no test-run report, no caching, and no cross-test-case parallelization -- which is fine, even desirable, for a quick debug loop. A (evaluate) is built for batch/parallel runs in scripts or notebooks. B (assert_test) is for CI/CD gating via pytest. D marks an official baseline run on Confident AI, overkill for a one-off debug.

question: In a pytest file using `@pytest.mark.parametrize("test_case", dataset.test_cases)` with `assert_test(test_case, [AnswerRelevancyMetric()])` inside the test function, what should you run at the command line -- and why not plain `pytest`?
options: A) Plain `pytest test_file.py` is fine and equivalent in every way
B) `deepeval test run test_file.py` -- it wraps pytest but adds async control, error handling, repeats, and run identifiers that plain pytest doesn't provide
C) `python test_file.py` directly, since deepeval doesn't integrate with pytest
D) `deepeval test run` only works without pytest.mark.parametrize
explanation: deepeval test run is pytest-native (it invokes pytest under the hood) but layers on deepeval-specific behavior: async execution control via AsyncConfig, structured error handling (skip vs fail on missing params), repeat-N-times support (-r flag), and a run identifier for tracking against Confident AI baselines. Running plain `pytest` will technically execute the assert_test calls, but you lose all of that orchestration -- which is why the docs and CI examples always show `deepeval test run`, never bare pytest. C is wrong -- deepeval is built around pytest.mark.parametrize as its dataset-looping idiom. D is a fabricated limitation.

question: `evaluate()` requires exactly 2 parameters and accepts several optional ones. Which pair is required?
options: A) dataset and hyperparameters
B) test_cases (or an EvaluationDataset) and metrics
C) identifier and async_config
D) golden and expected_output
explanation: evaluate() needs to know *what* to score (test_cases -- a list of LLMTestCase/ConversationalTestCase, or an EvaluationDataset) and *how* to score it (metrics -- the list of metric instances to run). Everything else -- hyperparameters, identifier, async_config, display_config, error_config, cache_config -- is optional configuration layered on top. A, C, and D each substitute an optional param for one of the two truly required ones.

question: A colleague says 'DeepEval and LangSmith do the same thing.' What's the sharpest correction, per deepeval's own framing?
options: A) They're identical -- both are observability tools
B) Evaluation != Observability: DeepEval scores 'is it good enough' (pass/fail against metrics); observability tools like LangSmith show 'what happened' (traces, logs, latency)
C) LangSmith is for scoring quality; DeepEval is only for logging traces
D) DeepEval replaces the need for any tracing or logging entirely
explanation: DeepEval's core value proposition is quality scoring: given a test case, does the output pass a metric's threshold? That's fundamentally different from observability tooling, which answers 'what happened during this run' -- traces, spans, latency, token counts -- without judging correctness. The two are complementary: deepeval's own tracing (@observe) borrows an observability-style mental model (traces/spans) specifically so metrics can be attached to what happened, bridging the two. B states this distinction correctly; C reverses the tools' actual roles, and A/D collapse a meaningful distinction that deepeval itself draws.

question: A ToolCall object used in `tools_called`/`expected_tools` supports which set of parameters?
options: A) name only -- no other fields exist
B) name (required) plus optional description, reasoning, output, and input_parameters
C) name and args only, mirroring OpenAI's function-calling schema exactly
D) name, latency, and cost -- used for operational monitoring
explanation: ToolCall's required field is name (which tool was invoked); description, reasoning, output, and input_parameters are all optional and let you capture richer context -- e.g. what arguments were passed (input_parameters) or what the tool returned (output) -- which unlocks stricter matching via ToolCorrectnessMetric's evaluation_params=[ToolCallParams.INPUT_PARAMETERS / OUTPUT] instead of just name-matching. B is correct; A undersells the object, C invents a nonexistent 'args' shorthand, and D confuses ToolCall with the separate token_cost/completion_time operational-logging fields on LLMTestCase.

question: You embed an image into a test case string for a multimodal metric using MLLMImage. What happens to that reference internally?
options: A) The image bytes are inlined directly into the JSON test case
B) It's converted into a `[DEEPEVAL:IMAGE:uuid]` slug embedded in the f-string, referencing the image out-of-band
C) MLLMImage is rejected unless the image is hosted on Confident AI first
D) Images can only be passed as separate top-level fields, never embedded in a string
explanation: MLLMImage lets you interleave images with text by embedding it inside an f-string; deepeval swaps that embed for a `[DEEPEVAL:IMAGE:uuid]` slug so the string stays serializable as a normal test-case field, with the actual image data tracked out-of-band and re-associated at eval/rendering time (via convert_to_multi_modal_array() to split it back out). This lets multimodal content flow through the same LLMTestCase/ConversationalTestCase/ArenaTestCase machinery all three support. A is wrong -- raw bytes aren't inlined into JSON. C invents a Confident-AI-only requirement. D is wrong -- embedding inside an f-string is exactly the supported pattern.

question: What is the relationship between an EvaluationDataset and a Golden?
options: A) A Golden is a fully-scored LLMTestCase; EvaluationDataset stores results after scoring
B) A Golden is an LLMTestCase minus actual_output/retrieval_context at creation time; EvaluationDataset is a collection of Goldens you convert to test cases by running your app
C) They're interchangeable names for the same object
D) EvaluationDataset stores only metric definitions, not data
explanation: A Golden captures the input (and optionally expected_output/context as static ground truth) but deliberately omits actual_output and retrieval_context, because those only exist once you actually run your live app against golden.input. EvaluationDataset(goldens=[...]) centralizes a batch of these so you can loop `dataset.add_test_case(LLMTestCase(input=golden.input, actual_output=your_app(golden.input)))` and then run many test cases against 1+ metrics in one place. A reverses the relationship -- Goldens are inputs, not scored outputs. C erases a meaningful distinction: you don't need a dataset just to test one case (assert_test/measure work standalone). D is wrong -- datasets hold data (goldens/test cases), not metric configs.

question: Which Synthesizer entry point skips document loading, chunking, and context grouping because you already supply pre-made context chunks?
options: A) generate_goldens_from_docs(document_paths=[...])
B) generate_goldens_from_scratch()
C) generate_goldens_from_contexts(contexts=[[...], [...]])
D) generate_goldens_from_csv_file()
explanation: generate_goldens_from_contexts() takes a list of pre-made context-chunk lists and jumps straight to golden generation + evolution, skipping the load-docs -> chunk -> group-into-contexts steps that generate_goldens_from_docs() runs in full starting from raw .txt/.docx/.pdf/.md/.mdx files. This is the right choice when you already have curated chunks (e.g. from an existing vector store) and don't want the synthesizer re-deriving context groupings via cosine similarity. B and D are not real Synthesizer entry points in this pipeline.

question: You call generate_goldens_from_docs with max_contexts_per_document=3 and num_evolutions=3, but no explicit max_goldens_per_context. The synthesizer produces far fewer goldens than expected. What's the most likely cause?
options: A) num_evolutions was set too high

B) max_contexts_per_document caps the contexts pulled per doc, and total goldens = max_contexts_per_document x max_goldens_per_context -- if your docs are short, chunk_size/chunk_overlap settings may not produce enough chunks to satisfy that cap
C) The synthesizer ignores max_contexts_per_document by design
D) Goldens are capped globally at 10 regardless of settings
explanation: Max goldens generated is the product of max_contexts_per_document and max_goldens_per_context, so undershooting on either factor -- most commonly because chunk_size is too large or chunk_overlap too small relative to a short document -- means there simply aren't enough distinct chunks to group into the requested number of contexts, and the synthesizer either errors or silently produces fewer contexts than the cap allows. A is a red herring -- num_evolutions controls per-golden complexity (up to 3 evolution steps sampled from 7 types), not count. C is false -- the cap is respected, just bottlenecked upstream by chunking. D invents a fixed ceiling that doesn't exist.

question: The Synthesizer's 7 evolution types split into 'vertical' and 'horizontal' axes. Which evolution is the horizontal one, and what does that distinction mean?
options: A) REASONING is horizontal -- it broadens topic coverage

B) IN_BREADTH is horizontal -- it broadens to adjacent/related topics, while the other six (REASONING, MULTICONTEXT, CONCRETIZING, CONSTRAINED, COMPARATIVE, HYPOTHETICAL) are vertical, making individual questions harder
C) CONSTRAINED is horizontal because it adds restrictions across multiple questions
D) All 7 evolutions are vertical; there is no horizontal axis
explanation: IN_BREADTH is the sole horizontal evolution: instead of making a single question harder, it broadens the golden set to cover adjacent/related topics -- widening coverage. The other six (REASONING, MULTICONTEXT, CONCRETIZING, CONSTRAINED, COMPARATIVE, HYPOTHETICAL) are all vertical: each makes an individual question harder along some axis (multi-step logic, forcing use of more context, concreteness, added constraints, comparison, hypothetical reasoning). The practical guidance is to mix both axes rather than overloading one, since vertical alone gives you hard-but-narrow coverage and horizontal alone gives you broad-but-shallow coverage.

question: The Synthesizer applies two quality gates during generation. What do they check, and what happens on failure?
options: A) They check grammar only, auto-correcting typos silently

B) Context filtering (clarity/depth/structure/relevance, per chunk) and synthetic input filtering (self-containment/clarity, per generated input) -- both scored 0-1 against a 0.5 threshold, with up to 3 retries
C) They check for duplicate goldens and delete exact matches
D) They validate against a JSON schema and reject malformed goldens
explanation: The two gates operate at different pipeline stages: context filtering happens per chunk at context-build time (is this chunk clear, deep, well-structured, and relevant enough to build a question from?), and synthetic input filtering happens per generated input (is the resulting question self-contained and clear on its own, without needing the chunk to make sense?). Both use a 0-1 score against a 0.5 threshold with up to 3 retries before giving up, and their scores are inspectable via golden.additional_metadata['context_quality'] / ['synthetic_input_quality']. B is accurate; the other options describe checks the synthesizer doesn't actually perform at this stage.

question: For loading goldens from an external source, which pairing is correct?
options: A) Single-turn uses dataset.pull(alias=...); multi-turn has no cloud pull support
B) Both single-turn and multi-turn support pulling from Confident AI via dataset.pull(alias=...) with the same call, just different underlying golden types
C) Only CSV loading is supported for multi-turn ConversationalGolden
D) JSON loading requires scenario_col_name but CSV loading does not support scenario fields at all
explanation: Dataset sourcing has 4 comparable paths that apply to both single-turn (Golden) and multi-turn (ConversationalGolden): in-code construction, pulling from Confident AI via dataset.pull(alias=...), and loading from CSV or JSON files -- just with different column/key names (input vs scenario/expected_outcome/user_description). The pull() call itself is identical in shape for both; only the alias differs. A and C both wrongly claim multi-turn lacks a capability single-turn has, and D is wrong -- CSV loading for ConversationalGolden explicitly supports scenario_col_name, expected_outcome_col_name, and user_description_col_name parameters.

question: When is it appropriate to reach for the Synthesizer instead of hand-writing goldens?
options: A) Only after your app is already in production and failing
B) When you don't have enough real examples yet -- to bootstrap edge cases before real users find them
C) Never -- synthetic data is always lower quality than human-written goldens
D) Only for safety metrics like Bias/Toxicity, never for RAG metrics
explanation: The Synthesizer's whole purpose is bootstrapping: when you're early in a project and don't yet have a rich set of real user queries, synthetic goldens let you exercise your evaluation pipeline and surface likely edge cases (via the 7 evolution types) before real traffic finds them for you. It's a stopgap for coverage, not a permanent replacement for real production data -- the self-improving loop from the theory addendum explicitly folds production failures back into your golden dataset over time. C overstates a real tradeoff into an absolute; A and D each invent an artificial restriction on when it's usable.

question: You don't need to build an EvaluationDataset at all in which scenario?
options: A) Whenever you're using any metric other than AnswerRelevancyMetric
B) When you're only testing a single, one-off test case -- assert_test() or metric.measure() work standalone without a dataset
C) Datasets are always mandatory in deepeval; there is no standalone mode
D) Only when running deepeval test run with the --official flag
explanation: EvaluationDataset exists to centralize running many test cases against one or more metrics -- but for a single test case, that overhead is unnecessary. assert_test(test_case, [metric]) and metric.measure(test_case) both work perfectly standalone, no dataset required. This matters practically: a quick debug session or a one-off sanity check doesn't need dataset scaffolding. B is correct; the other options each invent a hard requirement for datasets that doesn't exist.

question: Why would you wrap your system prompt in a deepeval Prompt object instead of just passing a raw string to your LLM call?
options: A) Prompt objects run faster than raw strings at inference time
B) A Prompt links to a test run via hyperparameters={"prompt": prompt}, attributing metric scores back to a specific prompt version -- enabling prompt-driven optimization
C) Raw strings are not supported by any deepeval metric
D) Prompt objects automatically translate the prompt into other languages
explanation: A Prompt is a template + model params bundle that becomes attributable: passing hyperparameters={"prompt": prompt} into evaluate() or logging it via @deepeval.log_hyperparameters lets you trace a given metric score back to exactly which prompt version produced it. That's what makes prompt-driven optimization possible -- you can compare score distributions across prompt_v1 vs prompt_v2 on Confident AI. A and D are fabricated capabilities. C is false -- raw strings work fine for the actual_output; the Prompt object is purely about attribution/versioning, not a metric requirement.

question: Component-level prompt evaluation (scoring one specific LLM span, not the whole app) is set up with:
options: A) evaluate(test_cases=[...], metrics=[AnswerRelevancyMetric()]) directly
B) @observe(type="llm", metrics=[AnswerRelevancyMetric()]) on the function, with update_llm_span(prompt=prompt_1) inside it -- run via evals_iterator() over a dataset, not evaluate()
C) assert_test(test_case, [AnswerRelevancyMetric()]) with no decorator needed
D) It isn't possible -- prompt attribution only works end-to-end
explanation: Component-level prompt eval requires the function to be an @observe(type="llm", ...)'d span, because update_llm_span(prompt=...) is only callable inside an LLM-typed span -- it's how you attribute a specific prompt to a specific generation step in a traced app. Since it's driving a traced app (not a flat evaluate() call), you iterate the dataset via evals_iterator() rather than passing precomputed test_cases to evaluate(). A and C describe end-to-end (not component-level) evaluation, which doesn't need tracing at all. D is wrong -- §6.2 explicitly shows this pattern works, just with tracing as a prerequisite.

question: Which additional param would you use on a Prompt to constrain the LLM's output to a structured pydantic schema?
options: A) ModelSettings.temperature
B) output_schema (a pydantic BaseModel), alongside output_type e.g. OutputType.SCHEMA
C) messages_template alone
D) verbosity
explanation: Prompt's output settings expose exactly two params for this: output_type (e.g. set to OutputType.SCHEMA to signal structured output is expected) and output_schema, which takes a pydantic BaseModel defining the structure. ModelSettings params like temperature/top_p/frequency_penalty control sampling behavior, not output structure. messages_template alone just defines the conversation template, with no structural enforcement. verbosity is one of ModelSettings' 9 params and controls response length/detail, not schema conformance.

question: Before referencing a Prompt in hyperparameters or update_llm_span, what must you do if it was sourced from a .json file or Confident AI?
options: A) Nothing -- it's usable immediately after Prompt() is constructed
B) Call .load() (for local files) or .pull() (for Confident AI) first -- deepeval throws otherwise
C) Manually parse the JSON yourself before wrapping it in a Prompt object
D) Set an environment variable PROMPT_SOURCE=file
explanation: Prompt().load(file_path="example.json") and Prompt(alias="X").pull(version="00.00.01") are the two calls that actually populate a Prompt object's content from an external source -- until one of them runs, the Prompt is an empty shell, and deepeval will throw if you try to use it in hyperparameters or update_llm_span before loading. This is a common footgun: constructing Prompt(alias="X") and immediately using it in hyperparameters without calling .pull() first. A is the exact mistake to avoid; C and D describe workflows deepeval doesn't require or support.

question: In the Model Context Protocol (MCP), what are the three roles, and how do clients and servers relate?
options: A) Host, Client, Server -- one client per server, but a host can run many clients
B) Publisher, Subscriber, Broker -- a pub/sub messaging model
C) Host, Server, Database -- servers connect directly to databases
D) Client, Server, Gateway -- gateways route between multiple hosts
explanation: MCP defines exactly three roles: Host (the app, e.g. Claude, that wants external context), Client (a 1:1 connection manager per server), and Server (which exposes context -- tools, resources, prompts). The relationship is strictly one client per server, but a single host can spin up many clients to talk to many servers simultaneously. This is Anthropic's open standard for LLM <-> external tools/data integration. B, C, and D invent role names and relationships that aren't part of the actual MCP spec.

question: What are the three primitives an MCP server exposes, and how are they fetched by a client session?
options: A) Functions, Variables, Events -- via session.list_functions()
B) Tools (actions), Resources (data), Prompts (templates) -- via ClientSession.list_tools() / .list_resources() / .list_prompts()
C) Models, Datasets, Metrics -- via session.list_models()
D) Read, Write, Execute -- via session.get_permissions()
explanation: MCP servers expose exactly three primitive types: Tools (callable actions), Resources (fetchable data), and Prompts (reusable templates). A client session discovers what's available via ClientSession.list_tools(), .list_resources(), and .list_prompts() respectively, and those results feed directly into deepeval's MCPServer object as available_tools, available_resources, and available_prompts. The other options invent primitive categories that don't correspond to the actual MCP spec or deepeval's MCPServer construction pattern.

question: When you call session.call_tool(name, args) at runtime and want to score it with deepeval, which object wraps that primitive call, and what fields does it capture?
options: A) ToolCall, with fields name and description only
B) MCPToolCall, with fields name, args, and result
C) MCPResourceCall, with fields uri and result
D) MCPPromptCall, with fields name and result only
explanation: The comparable trio in deepeval's MCP support wraps each primitive's runtime call into a matching object with the same shape (call the session method -> wrap result into the matching MCP*Call object): session.call_tool(name, args) -> MCPToolCall(name, args, result); session.read_resource(uri) -> MCPResourceCall(uri, result); session.get_prompt(name) -> MCPPromptCall(name, result). Option B correctly names both the object and its 3 fields for tool calls specifically. A confuses this with the plain ToolCall used for non-MCP agentic metrics. C and D correctly describe the *other* two objects but mislabel them as answering a tool-call question.

question: For multi-turn MCP evaluation with MultiTurnMCPMetric on a ConversationalTestCase, where do mcp_servers and the per-primitive call lists (mcp_tools_called, etc.) live?
options: A) Both live at the top-level ConversationalTestCase
B) mcp_servers is set once at the test-case level; the individual primitive-call lists (mcp_tools_called/mcp_resources_called/mcp_prompts_called) are set per-Turn, on assistant turns only
C) Both live inside each Turn, duplicated per turn
D) mcp_servers lives per-Turn; the call lists live at the test-case level
explanation: This is a deliberate placement split: mcp_servers describes what's available for the whole conversation, so it's set once at the ConversationalTestCase level. But which primitives were actually called happens turn-by-turn, so mcp_tools_called/mcp_resources_called/mcp_prompts_called are set per-Turn (and only meaningful on assistant turns, mirroring the general Turn rule for retrieval_context/tools_called). Getting this backwards -- e.g. putting mcp_servers on each Turn or the call lists at the top level -- is flagged explicitly as a common placement gotcha in deepeval's own docs.

question: What makes MCPUseMetric's evaluation special compared to a metric like ToolCorrectnessMetric when you pass it an LLMTestCase with an empty mcp_tools_called list?
options: A) It automatically fails the test case, since no tools were called
B) It judges whether calling ANY available primitive would have helped -- i.e. it can evaluate the decision to not use MCP at all, not just the quality of primitives that were used
C) It throws a validation error requiring at least one tool call
D) It defaults to a perfect score, since nothing went wrong
explanation: MCPUseMetric has a special case precisely for this scenario: given no called-primitive objects, it doesn't just shrug or auto-pass/fail -- it evaluates whether the agent *should* have used one of the available MCP primitives (from mcp_servers) to better answer the input, judging the abstention itself. This is a meaningfully different judgment from ToolCorrectnessMetric, which is deterministic name-matching against expected_tools and has nothing to say about whether tool use was appropriate in the first place. A, C, and D each assume a simplistic pass/fail-on-emptiness behavior that misses this nuance.

question: MultiTurnMCPUseMetric and MCPTaskCompletionMetric both operate on ConversationalTestCase with MCP servers attached. What's the process-vs-outcome distinction between them?
options: A) They measure the same thing; one is just deprecated
B) MultiTurnMCPUseMetric grades HOW MCP was used (right primitives, right args) averaged across the conversation; MCPTaskCompletionMetric grades WHETHER the task got done, per interaction, averaged
C) MultiTurnMCPUseMetric only works on single-turn cases despite the name
D) MCPTaskCompletionMetric requires mcp_servers to be omitted entirely
explanation: This mirrors the process-vs-outcome pattern that recurs across deepeval's metric families (Tool Correctness/Use vs Task Completion/Goal Accuracy): MultiTurnMCPUseMetric is about the mechanics of MCP usage -- did the agent pick the right primitives and pass sensible arguments across the conversation -- while MCPTaskCompletionMetric only cares whether the underlying task actually got accomplished, regardless of how clean the MCP usage was along the way. They're complementary, not redundant: a passing MCPTaskCompletionMetric alongside a failing MultiTurnMCPUseMetric tells you the agent got lucky or compensated rather than using MCP correctly. mcp_servers (list of available MCPServer) is mandatory on both.

question: DeepEval metrics are almost all LLM-as-judge, implemented via 3 techniques: QAG, DAG, and G-Eval. What does each stand for and do?
options: A) QAG = Quality Assurance Grading; DAG = Data Aggregation Graph; G-Eval = Generic Evaluation
B) QAG = Question-Answer-Generation; DAG = Deep Acyclic Graph decision tree; G-Eval = Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting-based scoring
C) QAG = Quantized Attention Gating; DAG = Directed Attention Graph; G-Eval = Gradient Evaluation
D) All three are marketing names for the same underlying technique
explanation: These are deepeval's three core LLM-judging techniques: QAG generates intermediate questions/answers to derive a score (used internally by metrics like Faithfulness/Answer Relevancy to extract claims/statements before judging them), DAG builds an explicit decision tree of judgement nodes for deterministic, path-based scoring (DAGMetric), and G-Eval uses chain-of-thought prompting against plain-English criteria for a holistic one-shot score (GEval). All output a 0-1 score plus a reason, and all pass if score >= threshold (default 0.5). The other options are fabricated expansions.

question: GEval requires you to provide exactly one of two mutually exclusive params. Which pair, and what's the tradeoff?
options: A) name XOR criteria -- name is required either way, criteria is decorative
B) criteria XOR evaluation_steps -- providing evaluation_steps skips CoT step-generation, giving more reproducible scores
C) threshold XOR strict_mode -- you can't set both a threshold and strict mode
D) model XOR evaluation_params -- these control the same underlying behavior
explanation: GEval's core tradeoff is criteria (plain-English description, e.g. 'Check whether facts contradict the expected output') vs evaluation_steps (an explicit, pre-written list of judgement steps). Passing criteria lets the judge LLM generate its own CoT steps at eval time -- flexible but slightly less reproducible run-to-run. Passing evaluation_steps directly skips that generation step, giving more deterministic, reproducible scoring since the reasoning path is fixed by you. You should never provide both. B correctly identifies this; the other options pair up params that aren't actually mutually exclusive or don't capture the real tradeoff.

question: DAGMetric is built from 4 node types. Which node type is the only kind of leaf, and what must every leaf provide?
options: A) TaskNode is the only leaf; it must provide instructions
B) VerdictNode is the only leaf type; it must provide either a score (0-10) XOR a child -- never both
C) BinaryJudgementNode is the only leaf; it must always have exactly 2 children
D) All 4 node types can be leaves interchangeably
explanation: VerdictNode is the leaf type in a DAG -- but note not every VerdictNode has to actually be a leaf; a VerdictNode can also delegate deeper by pointing to a child (another BaseNode or even a GEval metric), which is why the rule is score XOR child, never both. TaskNode processes/extracts data (e.g. pulling headings from actual_output) and always has children. BinaryJudgementNode gives a yes/no verdict with exactly 2 VerdictNode children (True/False), and NonBinaryJudgementNode gives an open-ended multi-class verdict with N VerdictNode children. Only B correctly identifies VerdictNode as the leaf type and its score-XOR-child constraint.

question: Why would you choose DAGMetric over a plain GEval for the same evaluation task?
options: A) DAGMetric is always faster since it makes fewer LLM calls
B) DAGMetric decomposes the judgement into explicit extract -> judge -> judge steps, leaving less room for the judge to hallucinate a score, vs GEval's one-shot holistic scoring
C) DAGMetric doesn't require an LLM judge at all -- it's fully rule-based
D) GEval cannot be used on LLMTestCase, only DAGMetric can
explanation: The core tradeoff: GEval asks the judge LLM to produce a single holistic score in one shot given criteria/steps, which is flexible but leaves room for an inconsistent or hallucinated number. DAGMetric forces the judgement through a fully deterministic decision tree of smaller, narrower sub-judgements (extract the relevant data, then judge specific yes/no or multi-class questions about it), which constrains the LLM to easier, narrower sub-tasks at each node -- reducing the chance of a wildly wrong final number, at the cost of needing to design the tree explicitly. B captures this correctly. C is wrong -- DAGMetric's judgement nodes (Binary/NonBinary) still call an LLM at each decision point; only the path traversal itself is deterministic. D is false -- both work fine on LLMTestCase.

question: ArenaGEval differs from the other 4 custom metric variants (GEval, ConversationalGEval, DAGMetric, ConversationalDAGMetric) in a fundamental way. What is it?
options: A) It's the only one that's deterministic

B) It picks a winner among contestants (relative scoring) rather than producing an absolute score-vs-threshold, has no threshold/strict_mode params, outputs .winner + .reason (no .score), and runs via compare() not evaluate()
C) It's the only one that supports multi-turn conversations
D) It's the only one that requires a custom DeepEvalBaseLLM judge
explanation: ArenaGEval is the odd one out among the 5 custom-metric variants because it operates on ArenaTestCase and answers 'which contestant is best' rather than 'does this one output pass a threshold' -- so it has no threshold or strict_mode (those only make sense for absolute scoring), its output is .winner plus .reason rather than .score, and it's invoked via compare(test_cases=[...], metric=arena_geval) instead of .measure()/evaluate(). It is non-deterministic (still LLM-judged) but bias-controlled via name-masking and order-randomization. It currently has no multi-turn equivalent -- only single-turn LLMTestCase contestants are supported.

question: What's the practical 'metric budget' guidance deepeval practitioners follow when selecting metrics for a single evaluation run, and why?
options: A) Use as many metrics as possible -- more coverage is always better
B) <=5 total: 2-3 generic system-specific metrics (RAG/agent/multi-turn) + 1-2 custom (GEval/DAG/self-coded) -- this forces prioritization and keeps judge cost/noise manageable
C) Exactly 1 metric per run, always
D) Only custom metrics should ever be used; built-ins are for demos only
explanation: The practical guidance caps a single run at roughly 5 metrics: a couple of the relevant system-specific built-ins (whichever RAG/agentic/chatbot metrics match your app's shape) plus 1-2 custom metrics for anything domain-specific a built-in doesn't cover. This isn't arbitrary -- every additional metric means another LLM judge call per test case (cost + latency), and an unfocused pile of metrics makes failure-mode debugging harder rather than easier since you're drowning in scores instead of acting on the few that matter. A ignores this real cost/signal tradeoff; C and D are overly rigid rules not reflected in actual practice.

question: Which distinction correctly separates reference-based from referenceless metrics, and why does it matter for production monitoring?
options: A) Reference-based metrics need ground truth (e.g. Contextual Recall, Tool Correctness); referenceless metrics don't (e.g. Task Completion, Step Efficiency, safety metrics) -- production/live monitoring must use referenceless metrics since no labeled data exists at runtime
B) Referenceless metrics are always less accurate and should be avoided in production
C) Reference-based metrics run faster since they skip the LLM judge call
D) The distinction only applies to RAG metrics, not agentic or safety metrics
explanation: Reference-based metrics compare actual behavior against a known-correct label (expected_output for Contextual Recall, expected_tools for Tool Correctness) -- fine offline where you curated goldens, but impossible in production where there's no ground truth for a live, novel user query. Referenceless metrics judge quality without needing that label (Task Completion judges against the inferred goal from the trace itself; safety metrics like Bias/Toxicity just inspect the output directly), which is exactly why they're the only viable option for scoring live traffic. B is wrong -- referencelessness is a structural necessity for production, not a quality downgrade. C and D misattribute the distinction.

question: Which properties from the 'common metric properties' set apply to virtually every deepeval metric?
options: A) threshold, strict_mode, verbose_mode, async_mode, include_reason, evaluation_template, model, .measure()/.a_measure(), .upload()
B) Only threshold and model -- the rest are metric-specific
C) chunk_size and chunk_overlap, since all metrics process retrieved chunks
D) num_evolutions, since all metrics are synthesizer-driven
explanation: This shared property set is what lets you avoid re-documenting configuration per metric: threshold (pass/fail cutoff, default 0.5), strict_mode (forces a binary 1/0, overriding threshold to 1), verbose_mode (prints intermediate reasoning), async_mode (default True, runs a metric's internal steps concurrently), include_reason (attach .reason alongside .score), evaluation_template (override the metric's default judge prompt, useful for weaker custom judges), model (judge LLM), .measure()/.a_measure() (sync/async standalone run), and .upload() (push a custom metric to Confident AI as reusable). C and D confuse metric configuration with Synthesizer configuration, which is a separate, unrelated concept.

question: You subclass AnswerRelevancyTemplate to override generate_statements() with a custom prompt, then pass evaluation_template=CustomTemplate to AnswerRelevancyMetric. Why might you do this?
options: A) To change the metric's threshold without using the threshold param
B) To help a weaker/custom LLM judge that produces more invalid-JSON errors with the metric's default prompt, by simplifying the in-context examples
C) To switch the metric from referenceless to reference-based
D) To disable async_mode for that metric only
explanation: evaluation_template exists precisely as an escape hatch for weaker or custom judge LLMs: deepeval's default prompts (and their in-context examples) are tuned for capable models like GPT-4, and a smaller/local judge (e.g. via Ollama) may struggle to reliably produce well-formed JSON from that prompt's complexity. Overriding the template to use simpler in-context examples reduces invalid-JSON parse failures. This is explicitly paired in the docs with -i/-c CLI flags (ignore-and-cache-skip) as the two levers for dealing with a flaky custom judge. A, C, and D each describe unrelated configuration knobs that evaluation_template doesn't touch.

question: Why does deepeval's documentation describe non-LLM statistical scorers (ROUGE/BLEU/BLEURT) as second-class citizens, not first-class documented metrics?
options: A) They aren't implemented at all anywhere in the codebase
B) They're only accessible by building a custom metric around the internal scorer module -- deepeval's stance is that they underperform LLM-judges for tasks requiring real reasoning
C) They require a paid Confident AI subscription to use
D) They only work on ConversationalTestCase, not LLMTestCase
explanation: ROUGE/BLEU/BLEURT-style n-gram/embedding-overlap scorers exist inside deepeval's internal scorer module, but they're not exposed as polished, documented, first-class metric classes the way FaithfulnessMetric or AnswerRelevancyMetric are -- you'd have to build a custom metric wrapping the scorer module yourself. This reflects a deliberate stance: these older NLP metrics measure surface-level lexical overlap, which correlates poorly with actual correctness/faithfulness for open-ended LLM outputs, so deepeval leans on LLM-as-judge for tasks that require real semantic reasoning. A is false -- the module exists, just isn't a headline feature. C and D are fabricated restrictions.

question: The RAG Triad refers to a specific set of 3 referenceless metrics. Which ones, and why is the Triad the go-to combo when you don't have labeled ground truth yet?
options: A) ContextualPrecisionMetric + ContextualRecallMetric + FaithfulnessMetric -- all reference-based
B) AnswerRelevancyMetric + FaithfulnessMetric + ContextualRelevancyMetric -- all referenceless, so high scores across all 3 signal a healthy end-to-end pipeline without needing expected_output
C) HallucinationMetric + ToxicityMetric + BiasMetric -- the 3 safety-critical metrics
D) AnswerRelevancyMetric + ContextualPrecisionMetric + ContextualRecallMetric
explanation: The RAG Triad is Answer Relevancy + Faithfulness + Contextual Relevancy -- deliberately the 3 RAG metrics that need no expected_output, meaning you can run them from day one on any test case that just has input/actual_output/retrieval_context. High scores across all 3 signal your pipeline is healthy end-to-end (generator answers on-topic and grounded, retriever pulls relevant signal) without requiring you to have curated ground-truth answers yet. Contextual Precision and Recall are deliberately excluded from the Triad because they're reference-based (need expected_output), making them the natural next step once you do have labeled data. A and D wrongly include reference-based metrics; C confuses the RAG Triad with unrelated safety metrics.

question: You observe low Faithfulness scores paired with HIGH Answer Relevancy on your RAG app. Per the failure-mode diagnostic grid, what's the likely root cause and fix?
options: A) Retriever pulled too much noise; fix is lowering top-K
B) Generator is confidently wrong, leaning on parametric (pretrained) knowledge over the retrieved evidence; fix is tightening the prompt to force grounding in retrieval_context
C) Retriever is missing info entirely; fix is raising top-K
D) Re-ranker is broken; fix is improving re-ranking/ordering
explanation: This specific pairing is a classic and dangerous failure mode: the answer is on-topic and relevant to the question (high Answer Relevancy) but not actually grounded in what was retrieved (low Faithfulness) -- meaning the LLM ignored or contradicted the retrieval_context and answered from its own parametric memory instead, sounding confident while being ungrounded. The fix is prompt-level: force the generator to cite/ground strictly in retrieval_context rather than falling back on pretrained knowledge. A, C, and D describe retriever-side symptoms (low Contextual Relevancy/Recall/Precision respectively), which is the wrong layer for this particular symptom pairing -- the retriever isn't implicated here since relevancy is fine, it's a generation-time faithfulness failure.

question: Contextual Precision uses a Weighted Cumulative Precision (WCP) formula rather than plain precision. Why does WCP weight top-ranked results more heavily?
options: A) To reduce the number of LLM judge calls needed
B) LLMs attend more to earlier context, so bad ranking increases downstream hallucination risk; WCP also handles graded relevance, not just binary retrieved/not-retrieved
C) Because retrieval systems always return exactly 10 results, and WCP is tuned for that count
D) To make the metric symmetric with Contextual Recall's formula
explanation: The formula Contextual Precision = (1/#relevant nodes) x Sum_k[(#relevant nodes up to position k / k) x r_k] weights each relevant node's contribution by how early it appears -- because generation-time attention tends to weight earlier context more heavily, so a relevant chunk buried at position 8 is functionally less useful (and riskier) than the same chunk at position 1, even though plain precision would score them identically. It also generalizes to graded relevance rather than pure binary retrieved/not-retrieved, since r_k represents binary relevance of the k-th node but the cumulative weighting still captures 'how well-ranked' the useful nodes are. A, C, and D are fabricated justifications unrelated to the actual mechanism.

question: Why does ContextualRecallMetric attribute statements from expected_output rather than actual_output when checking retrieval_context coverage?
options: A) It's a bug that's scheduled to be fixed in a future version
B) So a bad generator can't unfairly drag down a good retriever's recall score -- Recall should isolate retriever completeness, not generation quality
C) expected_output is easier to parse than actual_output
D) actual_output is never available at the time Contextual Recall runs
explanation: This is a deliberate design choice for metric isolation: if Contextual Recall extracted statements from actual_output instead, a generator that failed to use good retrieved context (a generation-layer problem) would make the retriever look bad too, muddying which pipeline stage actually failed. By attributing against expected_output -- your curated ground-truth ideal answer -- Contextual Recall answers a clean question: 'does retrieval_context contain everything needed to have produced the ideal answer?', independent of whether the generator actually used it well that run. A and D are false; C is a superficial, incorrect justification for a deliberate architectural decision.

question: Which RAG metric is the only one of the 5 that ignores actual_output entirely, and what does it check instead?
options: A) FaithfulnessMetric -- checks retrieval_context against context
B) ContextualRelevancyMetric -- checks a pure input <-> retrieval_context topical/signal-to-noise relationship, referenceless
C) AnswerRelevancyMetric -- checks input against expected_output
D) ContextualPrecisionMetric -- checks actual_output against retrieval_context ranking
explanation: ContextualRelevancyMetric is scoped purely to the retriever: is retrieval_context relevant to input, checking for noise (irrelevant chunks that snuck into what was retrieved)? It never looks at actual_output at all, which is what makes it the only RAG metric with that property -- it's a pure retriever-quality signal, referenceless, and evaluates signal-to-noise ratio in what was pulled back. A, C, and D each misdescribe a different RAG metric's actual required fields -- Faithfulness needs actual_output+retrieval_context, Answer Relevancy needs input+actual_output, and Contextual Precision needs retrieval_context+expected_output (not actual_output).

question: You need to diagnose whether your reranker is doing its job (as opposed to your embedding model or chunk size). Which metric symptom most directly points to a reranking problem?
options: A) Low Contextual Recall alone
B) Low Contextual Precision paired with HIGH Contextual Recall -- the right chunks are being retrieved (recall is fine) but poorly ranked
C) Low Answer Relevancy alone
D) Low Faithfulness paired with low Contextual Relevancy
explanation: This pairing isolates the reranking stage specifically: high Contextual Recall confirms the right chunks ARE somewhere in retrieval_context (so embedding model + top-K/chunk size are working), but low Contextual Precision means those relevant chunks aren't ranked near the top -- exactly the reranker's job. The fix lever is improving re-ranker/ordering, not touching retrieval breadth. A alone (low recall) points to embedding model or top-K/chunk-size issues instead -- missing info entirely, not an ordering problem. C points to generation-side prompt/logic issues. D describes a generator-confidence problem plus noisy retrieval, unrelated to reranking specifically.

question: FaithfulnessMetric has a known structured-output bug on gpt-4o-mini leading to 16k-token runaway completions. What was the pragmatic hands-on workaround noted for a related check?
options: A) Switch to HallucinationMetric as the practical substitute, since it checks actual_output against a separate ground-truth context rather than requiring the same structured extraction
B) Disable async_mode on FaithfulnessMetric to avoid the bug
C) Always set threshold=1.0 to force strict_mode and bypass the bug
D) Switch judge models to Claude, which fixes the bug entirely
explanation: Faithfulness checks actual_output against retrieval_context (RAG-specific groundedness), while Hallucination checks actual_output against a separate ground-truth context field -- different field, different check, but similar spirit ('is this answer made up'). When Faithfulness hit a structured-output bug with gpt-4o-mini causing runaway 16k-token completions, the practical workaround documented from hands-on experience was substituting HallucinationMetric where groundedness-checking was the goal, since its extraction pattern didn't trigger the same bug. B, C, and D are plausible-sounding but fabricated fixes not reflected in the actual documented workaround.

question: Which RAG pipeline hyperparameter is diagnosed by Contextual Recall specifically, according to the stage-to-hyperparameter mapping?
options: A) top-K / chunk size -- 'is it retrieving the right amount of info?'
B) reranker -- 'is the ordering correct?'
C) embedding model -- 'does it capture domain-specific nuance?'
D) LLM choice -- 'does it hallucinate against retrieval_context?'
explanation: The documented stage -> hyperparameter -> metric mapping ties Contextual Recall to the embedding model specifically: recall failures (missing relevant info entirely from retrieval_context) most often trace back to an embedding model that doesn't capture domain-specific nuance well enough to retrieve the truly relevant chunks in the first place, no matter how top-K or chunk size are tuned. top-K/chunk size maps to Contextual Relevancy (retrieving the right amount, not too noisy); reranker maps to Contextual Precision (ordering); LLM choice maps to Faithfulness (hallucination against retrieval_context). Getting this mapping right is what lets you point a low score directly at the lever to pull.

question: 'The Interaction Trap' is a specific workflow-level RAG failure example used to answer 'give me a case where components pass individually but the system still fails.' What is it?
options: A) The retriever times out under load, causing a cascading failure across all downstream components

B) The retriever fetches the right document AND a wrong one; the generator picks the wrong one to answer from -- Faithfulness alone won't catch this, you need Contextual Precision (ranking) working WITH Faithfulness to see the workflow-level fault
C) The generator caches a stale response from a previous unrelated query
D) Two different embedding models disagree on the same query, causing a version conflict
explanation: This is the sharpest example of why component-level pass/fail isn't sufficient: the retriever technically 'worked' (the right document IS somewhere in retrieval_context, so a naive recall check might even pass), and the generator technically 'worked' (it faithfully reflects SOME retrieved chunk, so Faithfulness alone could pass too) -- but the generator picked the wrong chunk to build its answer from, and neither single component-level metric catches that interaction. You need Contextual Precision (does ranking put the right chunk first) working together with Faithfulness (is the answer grounded in what was used) to expose this workflow-level fault, which sits at the 'do components work together' level above pure per-component scoring. This is a strong rehearsed interview answer, not something to reconstruct on the fly.

question: Which of these is NOT a required LLMTestCase field for AnswerRelevancyMetric?
options: A) input
B) actual_output
C) retrieval_context
D) All three are required
explanation: AnswerRelevancyMetric only requires input and actual_output -- it checks whether the generated answer is relevant to what was asked, which is purely a generator-side, referenceless check that doesn't need to inspect what was retrieved at all. This is what makes it the 'baseline' entry in the RAG metric family: the only two-field metric in the whole RAG set. retrieval_context becomes necessary the moment you move to Faithfulness (checks actual_output against retrieval_context) or any Contextual* metric (all scoped to retriever quality), but it's not needed here.

question: Comparing Faithfulness and Answer Relevancy as the 'generator pair': what do they have in common, and how do they differ?
options: A) Both are reference-based and require expected_output
B) Both are referenceless and extract statements/claims from actual_output -- but Answer Relevancy checks those claims against input, while Faithfulness checks them against retrieval_context
C) Both check retrieval_context against context
D) Faithfulness is referenceless; Answer Relevancy is reference-based
explanation: Both metrics extract claims/statements from actual_output using the same QAG-style extraction pattern, and both are referenceless -- neither needs expected_output. The distinction is what they check those extracted claims against: Answer Relevancy checks 'is this claim relevant to what the user asked (input)?' while Faithfulness checks 'is this claim actually supported by what was retrieved (retrieval_context), i.e. not hallucinated?' Same formula shape (# relevant/faithful statements / total), applied against different reference points. A and D get the reference-based/referenceless status backwards or wrong; C confuses this pair with retriever-side metrics entirely.

question: How is ContextualRelevancyMetric's formula shape related to AnswerRelevancyMetric's, and what does that reveal about their role in the pipeline?
options: A) They share no structural similarity
B) They share the same formula shape (# relevant statements / total) but apply it to opposite ends of the pipeline -- retrieval_context (Contextual Relevancy) vs actual_output (Answer Relevancy)
C) Contextual Relevancy is a strict superset that includes Answer Relevancy's check
D) Answer Relevancy computes a ratio; Contextual Relevancy computes a raw count
explanation: Both metrics use the same underlying shape -- a ratio of 'relevant statements' to 'total statements' -- but they apply that lens at opposite pipeline boundaries: Contextual Relevancy asks it of retrieval_context (is what came IN from the retriever relevant/low-noise?), while Answer Relevancy asks it of actual_output (is what went OUT to the user relevant?). Recognizing this symmetry is useful for building intuition fast: once you understand one relevancy-style metric's mechanism, you understand the shape of the other, just pointed at a different pipeline stage. C and D invent false relationships; A misses a genuinely useful structural parallel.

question: Faithfulness-only extras include truths_extraction_limit and penalize_ambiguous_claims. What does each control?
options: A) truths_extraction_limit sets the judge model's temperature; penalize_ambiguous_claims disables async_mode

B) truths_extraction_limit caps how many truths are pulled from retrieval_context (ranked by importance); penalize_ambiguous_claims controls whether ambiguous claims count against faithfulness (default False -- they don't)
C) Both control the metric's threshold value directly
D) truths_extraction_limit is deprecated in favor of chunk_size
explanation: truths_extraction_limit caps how many ground-truth 'truths' get pulled from retrieval_context during the extraction step, ranked by importance -- useful for capping judge cost/noise on very long retrieval contexts. penalize_ambiguous_claims controls whether a claim that's ambiguous (neither clearly faithful nor clearly contradictory) should count against the faithfulness score; by default (False) ambiguous claims are NOT counted as unfaithful, giving the generator benefit of the doubt on genuinely unclear cases. Neither param touches temperature, async_mode, or threshold directly, ruling out A and C; D is a fabricated deprecation.

question: Given the pipeline-stage diagnostic table, low Answer Relevancy alone (with everything else healthy) most directly points to a problem with which lever?
options: A) The prompt template -- does it instruct the LLM to use retrieval_context well?
B) The embedding model
C) The reranker
D) top-K / chunk size
explanation: Answer Relevancy maps to the prompt template hyperparameter at the generation stage -- when the answer is off-topic, rambling, or hedging (the classic low-Answer-Relevancy symptom per the failure-mode grid), the fix lever documented is tightening prompt/generation logic, i.e. making sure the prompt instructs the LLM to actually use the retrieved context and answer the specific question asked, rather than wandering. B, C, and D are all retrieval-stage levers (embedding model -> Contextual Recall, reranker -> Contextual Precision, top-K/chunk size -> Contextual Relevancy) and wouldn't be the first place to look for a pure Answer Relevancy symptom with everything else healthy.

question: The mental model for single-turn agentic metrics splits agent failure into 3 layers. What are they, and which metrics map to each?
options: A) Input/Output/Latency -- no metrics map cleanly to these

B) Reasoning (plans/decides tool order -> PlanQuality/PlanAdherence), Action (selects tools/generates args -> ToolCorrectness/ArgumentCorrectness), Execution (orchestrates the loop end to end -> TaskCompletion/StepEfficiency)
C) Retrieval/Generation/Ranking -- borrowed directly from RAG
D) Perception/Planning/Actuation -- classic robotics terms with no deepeval mapping
explanation: This 3-layer framing is a strong interview soundbite: Reasoning layer covers planning/decomposition/tool-ordering decisions (PlanQualityMetric judges if the plan itself is good; PlanAdherenceMetric judges if execution followed that plan), Action layer covers the actual tool selection and argument generation (ToolCorrectnessMetric is deterministic name-matching; ArgumentCorrectnessMetric is LLM-judged argument sensibility), and Execution/Overall layer covers whether the full reasoning<->action loop actually reached the goal (TaskCompletionMetric judges outcome; StepEfficiencyMetric judges whether execution was lean). Combining one metric from each layer gives full-stack coverage instead of a partial, misleading picture.

question: A test run shows TaskCompletionMetric passing but ToolCorrectnessMetric failing on the same trace. What does this combination actually tell you?
options: A) The metrics are contradictory and one must be misconfigured
B) The agent got lucky or compensated for a wrong tool choice rather than executing correctly -- the outcome was fine, but the process that got there wasn't
C) TaskCompletionMetric is unreliable and should be discarded
D) This combination is impossible; deepeval would raise a validation error
explanation: This is exactly the scenario the '4 orthogonal lenses on the same trace' guidance warns about: TaskCompletion is outcome-only (did we reach the goal), while ToolCorrectness is process-only (were the right tools called). A passing outcome with a failing process usually means the agent got lucky (e.g. called the wrong tool but the environment happened to return usable data anyway) or compensated through some other path -- which is a real reliability risk even though the single trace 'succeeded'. This is precisely why you combine one Reasoning/Action metric with one Execution metric rather than relying on outcome-only signals, which can mask fragile agent behavior. B is the correct read; the other options misinterpret what's a meaningful, expected combination.

question: Which single-turn agentic metric is deterministic-first and can be used on a plain LLMTestCase with .measure(), with no tracing/@observe setup required at all?
options: A) TaskCompletionMetric
B) StepEfficiencyMetric
C) ToolCorrectnessMetric
D) PlanQualityMetric
explanation: ToolCorrectnessMetric is the cheapest agentic metric to adopt because it's the only one of the 6 that works standalone against a plain LLMTestCase carrying tools_called/expected_tools -- no @observe decoration or trace needed. It's mostly deterministic (name-matching, with an optional LLM check layered on for stricter matching). TaskCompletionMetric, StepEfficiencyMetric, PlanAdherenceMetric, and PlanQualityMetric are all trace-only -- they need the full trace from a traced agent function and only run via evals_iterator(metrics=[...]) or @observe, never standalone via .measure().

question: PlanQuality and PlanAdherence are described as a pair worth naming together in interviews. What's the precise distinction between them?
options: A) Quality checks if tools were called correctly; Adherence checks if arguments were correct
B) Quality judges the plan BEFORE execution (was it logical/complete/efficient); Adherence judges fidelity DURING execution (did the agent stick to its own plan)
C) They're synonyms; only one needs to be reported
D) Quality is reference-based; Adherence is referenceless
explanation: This is a documented interview soundbite worth memorizing verbatim: 'Quality judges the plan before execution, Adherence judges fidelity during execution.' PlanQualityMetric evaluates whether the plan itself -- pulled from the agent's thinking/reasoning span -- is logical, complete, and efficient, entirely ignoring whether execution actually followed it (it auto-scores 1 if no plan is found at all). PlanAdherenceMetric compares the plan against the actual execution steps taken, to catch cases where an agent devises a great plan but then ignores it (low Adherence, high Quality) or a mediocre plan that gets executed faithfully (high Adherence, low Quality) -- running both tells them apart. A and D misattribute the distinction to unrelated axes.

question: How does ArgumentCorrectnessMetric fundamentally differ from ToolCorrectnessMetric in what 'correct' means?
options: A) Tool Correctness is LLM-judged and referenceless; Argument Correctness is deterministic name-matching

B) Tool Correctness is deterministic name-matching against expected_tools ('right tool'); Argument Correctness is LLM-judged, referenceless, and asks whether arguments logically fit the input ('right inputs to that tool'), with no hardcoded correct answer
C) They evaluate identical things; Argument Correctness is just the newer name
D) Argument Correctness only runs on MCP-based tool calls, not regular ToolCall objects
explanation: Another documented soundbite: 'Tool Correctness asks right tool, Argument Correctness asks right inputs to that tool.' ToolCorrectnessMetric is deterministic by design -- it name-matches tools_called against expected_tools (optionally checking ordering or input_parameters/output too). ArgumentCorrectnessMetric is LLM-judged and referenceless -- there's no hardcoded 'correct' argument value to match against; instead the judge assesses whether the arguments passed to a tool make sense given the input, catching cases where the right tool was picked but fed nonsensical or poorly-derived arguments. A reverses the determinism assignment; C and D are false.

question: For production monitoring of an agent, how do you swap from local dev-time metrics to Confident-AI-hosted async scoring on live traffic, and what changes in your code?
options: A) You rewrite the entire @observe-decorated function to remove tracing

B) Swap a local metrics=[...] list for a Confident-AI-hosted metric_collection string on the same @observe decorator, e.g. @observe(metric_collection="my-agent-metrics") -- same span, no other code change, scores live traffic asynchronously with zero added latency
C) You must switch from @observe to a separate @monitor decorator
D) Production monitoring requires disabling tracing and using log files instead
explanation: This is one of deepeval's cleanest production-readiness features: the exact same @observe-decorated span you used for dev-time metrics=[...] scoring can instead reference a metric_collection string (a named collection configured on Confident AI), and that's the only code change needed. The scoring then happens asynchronously against live traffic with zero added latency to the actual request, since it's not blocking the response path. A, C, and D each describe unnecessary rewrites; the whole point of this design is that it's a one-line swap, not an architecture change.

question: Which agentic metrics can run together via evals_iterator(metrics=[...]) on the SAME trace, since they're described as 4 orthogonal lenses?
options: A) Only ToolCorrectnessMetric and ArgumentCorrectnessMetric
B) TaskCompletionMetric, StepEfficiencyMetric, PlanAdherenceMetric, and PlanQualityMetric
C) Only one metric can be attached per evals_iterator() call
D) TaskCompletionMetric and ToolCorrectnessMetric are mutually exclusive and can't run together
explanation: TaskCompletion, StepEfficiency, PlanAdherence, and PlanQuality are explicitly framed as 4 orthogonal lenses on the same trace -- outcome, execution leanness, plan fidelity, and plan quality respectively -- and they're designed to run together via a single evals_iterator(metrics=[m1, m2, m3, m4]) call against the same traced agent function, since none of them work standalone via .measure() anyway (they need the full trace regardless). This is different from ToolCorrectness, which CAN run standalone. B is correct; the other options invent restrictions that don't reflect how these metrics are actually meant to be composed.

question: What does the 'Formula' column reveal about how TaskCompletionMetric and StepEfficiencyMetric are both scored under the hood?
options: A) Both use a raw pass/fail count with no scoring nuance

B) Both use an AlignmentScore(...) formula -- TaskCompletion computes AlignmentScore(Task, Outcome); StepEfficiency computes AlignmentScore(Task, Execution Steps) -- an LLM-judged alignment between the task and some aspect of what happened
C) Both are computed via cosine similarity between embeddings
D) Neither has a defined formula; scores are purely qualitative
explanation: Both metrics share the same underlying AlignmentScore mechanism -- an LLM-judged assessment of how well one thing aligns with another -- just pointed at different targets: TaskCompletionMetric computes AlignmentScore(Task, Outcome) to judge whether what actually happened accomplishes the (auto-inferred-from-trace, if not given) task/goal, while StepEfficiencyMetric computes AlignmentScore(Task, Execution Steps) to judge whether the steps taken were lean and non-redundant relative to that same task. Recognizing the shared AlignmentScore pattern is useful for quickly understanding new metrics in this family without memorizing each in isolation.

question: PlanAdherenceMetric and PlanQualityMetric both have an 'auto-1-if-no-plan-found' rule. Why might this matter in practice?
options: A) It means agents that don't explicitly plan will always score perfectly on these metrics, which can mask agents that should be planning but aren't
B) It means the metric throws a hard error if no plan is detected in the trace
C) It's irrelevant -- all agents always produce an explicit plan
D) It only applies to PlanQualityMetric, not PlanAdherenceMetric
explanation: Since both metrics auto-score 1 (perfect) when no plan is found in the trace's thinking/reasoning span, a naive reactive agent that never explicitly plans (just reacts turn-by-turn without an articulated plan) would score perfectly on both -- which can be misleading if you actually expected the agent architecture to produce explicit plans and it silently isn't. This is a real gotcha worth knowing: a perfect PlanQuality/PlanAdherence score doesn't automatically mean 'this agent plans well,' it might mean 'this agent isn't planning at all and the metric can't penalize an absence.' B, C, and D misstate the actual documented behavior.

question: ToolCorrectnessMetric supports should_consider_ordering and should_exact_match params. What's the relationship between them?
options: A) They're independent and can be freely combined in any configuration
B) should_exact_match overrides ordering behavior and requires the tools_called and expected_tools lists to be identical
C) should_consider_ordering is ignored entirely if available_tools isn't set
D) Both default to True and cannot be disabled
explanation: should_exact_match is the stricter of the two: turning it on requires tools_called to be an identical list match against expected_tools, which by definition also fixes ordering (an identical list has a fixed order), so it effectively overrides/subsumes should_consider_ordering's more lenient 'same tools, but does order matter' check. should_consider_ordering alone lets you require the right tools in the right sequence without demanding the lists be otherwise identical (e.g. same length, no extras). Also worth knowing: passing available_tools unlocks an additional LLM-judged tool-selection-optimality check layered on top of the deterministic match. A, C, and D misdescribe these params' actual interaction and defaults.

question: When attaching agentic metrics to spans, which layer(s) are attached end-to-end (via evals_iterator(metrics=[...]) needing the full trace) versus component-level (via @observe(type="llm", metrics=[...]) on the specific span)?
options: A) All 6 agentic metrics are always component-level only

B) Reasoning/Execution metrics (Plan*, TaskCompletion, StepEfficiency) attach end-to-end since they need the full trace; Action metrics (ToolCorrectness, ArgumentCorrectness) attach component-level on the specific LLM span where tool/argument decisions are made
C) All 6 agentic metrics are always end-to-end only
D) The split is randomly assigned per project, not architecturally determined
explanation: This split follows directly from what each metric needs to see: Reasoning and Execution layer metrics (PlanQuality, PlanAdherence, TaskCompletion, StepEfficiency) need to reason about the whole trajectory -- the full trace -- so they attach at the trace level via evals_iterator(metrics=[...]). Action layer metrics (ToolCorrectness, ArgumentCorrectness) are about a specific decision point -- which tool, which arguments -- so they're naturally attached component-level via @observe(type="llm", metrics=[...]) on the specific LLM span where that decision happens, mirroring the same end-to-end vs component-level split used elsewhere in deepeval (e.g. for prompt evaluation).

question: Given the metric.measure(test_case) style Standalone-vs-traced architecture note, which of the 6 agentic metrics is the SOLE row that stays outside the '@observe agent function; only the evals_iterator(metrics=[...]) list changes' pattern?
options: A) TaskCompletionMetric
B) ToolCorrectnessMetric
C) PlanAdherenceMetric
D) ArgumentCorrectnessMetric
explanation: Per the documented architecture note: 'Row 1 [ToolCorrectnessMetric] -> plain metric.measure(test_case), no tracing needed. Rows 2-7 -> same @observe agent function; only the evals_iterator(metrics=[...]) list changes.' ToolCorrectnessMetric is the sole exception because it's deterministic-first and works off tools_called/expected_tools directly on a plain LLMTestCase -- it doesn't need to inspect a trace at all. TaskCompletion, StepEfficiency, PlanAdherence, PlanQuality, and ArgumentCorrectness (note: ArgumentCorrectness technically also works on a plain LLMTestCase per later notes, but is grouped with the traced rows in this particular architecture table) all follow the shared @observe pattern where only the metrics list swaps.

question: The 'Turn*' metric family (TurnRelevancyMetric, TurnFaithfulnessMetric, etc.) are multi-turn mirrors of the single-turn RAG metrics. What's the one genuinely new mechanism they introduce?
options: A) They use a completely different LLM judging technique (DAG instead of QAG)
B) A sliding window of turns (window_size, default 10) -- each window is scored like the single-turn equivalent, then averaged across the conversation (sum per-window scores / total assistant turns)
C) They require expected_output on every turn
D) They only run in strict_mode, unlike their single-turn equivalents
explanation: The single genuinely new concept versus single-turn RAG metrics is the sliding window: instead of scoring the whole conversation as one blob, each Turn* metric scores a window of recent turns (window_size, default 10) using essentially the same mechanism as its single-turn equivalent (e.g. TurnFaithfulnessMetric mirrors FaithfulnessMetric), then averages those per-window scores across the conversation -- formula shape is 'sum of per-window scores / total assistant turns', mirroring the single-turn formula but applied inside each window. A is false -- the underlying judging technique per window is unchanged. C is wrong -- only the Precision/Recall variants need a reference field, not all 5. D is fabricated.

question: TurnContextualPrecisionMetric and TurnContextualRecallMetric need an extra reference field beyond what the other 3 Turn* metrics need. Which field, and what's the naming gotcha?
options: A) expected_output, same name as the single-turn LLMTestCase field -- no naming risk
B) expected_outcome -- the singular, test-case-level field on ConversationalTestCase (same field used elsewhere by scenario), easily confused with the single-turn expected_output
C) golden_reference -- a brand-new field unique to these two metrics
D) They don't need any extra field beyond the other 3 Turn* metrics
explanation: This is an explicitly flagged gotcha: single-turn Precision/Recall metrics use expected_output (per LLMTestCase), but their Turn-prefixed multi-turn versions use expected_outcome -- the same singular, test-case-level field that ConversationalTestCase already uses elsewhere (alongside scenario) to describe what success looks like for the whole conversation. The near-identical spelling (expected_output vs expected_outcome) makes this an easy typo to make, and using the wrong one will silently fail or error depending on context. A and C invent incorrect field names; D wrongly claims no extra field is needed.

question: Which pure chatbot-quality metric (not RAG-based) is described as 'the odd one out' because its threshold behaves differently from the other two in its group?
options: A) RoleAdherenceMetric -- needs chatbot_role
B) ConversationCompletenessMetric -- needs no extra field
C) KnowledgeRetentionMetric -- strict_mode=True sets threshold to 0 (every other metric sets it to 1), since it's counting attritions and a single forgotten fact should fail the case outright
D) All 3 behave identically with threshold defaults
explanation: KnowledgeRetentionMetric is explicitly flagged as the odd one out among RoleAdherenceMetric, KnowledgeRetentionMetric, and ConversationCompletenessMetric: because its formula counts attritions (# assistant turns WITHOUT knowledge attrition / total assistant turns), a single instance of the assistant forgetting a fact the user already gave is serious enough that strict_mode setting the threshold to 0 (rather than the usual 1) is the intended behavior -- meaning that with strict_mode on, ANY single forgotten fact fails the whole test case outright, unlike the more forgiving threshold=1 convention used elsewhere. A and B correctly describe those metrics' extra-field requirements but don't answer the threshold-quirk question asked.
