explanation: MAE (Mean Absolute Error) between the LLM-judge's numeric scores and human expert scores on the same set of outputs is the documented, named, quantified metric for this -- much stronger as an interview answer than a vague 'we compare to humans' because it demonstrates you have an actual measurement, not just a process description. The framing is explicit: the goal is driving MAE toward zero, at which point the LLM judge becomes trustworthy enough to serve as a reliable, low-cost proxy for expensive human expert review at scale. C and D invent alternative or fabricated metrics not reflected in the documented material; A names a real metric (F1) but one used for classification agreement, not the score-drift use case described here.

question: Which 5 styles of human evaluation should you name if asked 'how do you use humans in your eval pipeline beyond labeling goldens?'
options: A) Unit testing, integration testing, regression testing, smoke testing, load testing
B) Direct Grading/Rating, Red Teaming (attacking the system), A/B Testing, Golden Dataset Creation, Human-in-the-Loop
C) Bias review, toxicity review, PII review, misuse review, role-violation review
D) Precision checking, recall checking, F1 validation, latency review, cost review
explanation: This is a memorize-verbatim list for interview readiness: Direct Grading/Rating (humans score outputs directly against a rubric), Red Teaming (humans actively attacking the system to find vulnerabilities, distinct from automated RedTeamer scans), A/B Testing (comparing variants with real user outcomes), Golden Dataset Creation (the human labeling work most people default to when asked this question), and Human-in-the-Loop (humans reviewing/correcting individual outputs as part of an ongoing production workflow). The documented advice is explicit: 'name these five, don't just say human review' -- a generic answer signals shallower familiarity with the space than naming the specific taxonomy. A, C, and D are fabricated or unrelated lists.

question: 'Captured vs Computed' signals sharpen the vague idea of 'running referenceless metrics on production traces' into two distinct types. What's the distinction, and which one maps to DeepEval's metric_collection on @observe?
options: A) Captured = LLM-judge scores on sampled traces; Computed = thumbs up/down and latency -- metric_collection is Captured

B) Captured = passive signals (thumbs up/down, latency, cost) -- no LLM call, free; Computed = proactive signals (LLM-as-judge running Faithfulness/Hallucination on sampled traces) -- this is what metric_collection on @observe does for the Computed half
C) Captured and Computed are synonyms; the distinction is purely stylistic
D) Captured signals require Confident AI login; Computed signals work fully offline
explanation: This is precise vocabulary for a fuzzy-sounding practice: Captured signals are PASSIVE -- things you already have for free from normal operation (thumbs up/down feedback, latency, cost) with no LLM call needed to obtain them. Computed signals are PROACTIVE -- you deliberately run an LLM-as-judge (e.g. Faithfulness, Hallucination) against a SAMPLE of production traces to actively assess quality, which costs money per evaluation. The interview line ties this directly to a concrete mechanism: 'In production I capture passive signals for free, and compute LLM-judge signals on a sample -- that's exactly what DeepEval's @observe(metric_collection=...) does for the computed half.' A reverses the definitions; D invents a false dependency on Confident AI login.

question: 'Stratified Sampling' names a specific strategy already implicit in a 'sample 5-20% + all errors' CI approach. What does stratified sampling actually prioritize, and why say the term explicitly?
options: A) It prioritizes purely random sampling across all traffic equally, to avoid any bias

B) It prioritizes sampling FROM PROBLEMATIC CATEGORIES (negative feedback, escalated chats) over pure random sampling, to control judge cost while still catching real issues; naming the term signals a deliberate strategy, not an ad hoc shortcut
C) It only applies to safety metrics, never to quality metrics
D) It requires sampling exactly 50% of all traffic at all times
explanation: Stratified sampling means deliberately over-weighting your sample toward categories more likely to contain real problems -- negative user feedback, escalated support chats, categories with historically higher failure rates -- rather than sampling uniformly at random across all traffic, which would waste judge-LLM budget re-confirming that mostly-fine traffic is fine while under-sampling the traffic most likely to reveal genuine issues. The documentation explicitly notes: saying the term 'stratified sampling' out loud in an interview signals this was a deliberate architectural choice on your part, rather than an unnamed, accidental shortcut you happened to land on. A describes plain random sampling, the opposite of the strategy being named; C and D invent false restrictions.

question: 'Data Drift' is distinct from a model getting worse. What does Data Drift actually refer to, and why does it matter for golden datasets specifically?
options: A) Data Drift means your vector database physically corrupts over time

B) Data Drift means business reality (pricing, policy, curriculum, etc.) changes UNDERNEATH a fixed golden dataset, silently making yesterday's correct answer today's wrong one -- this is why golden datasets need refresh cycles, not just regression testing
C) Data Drift only refers to embedding model version upgrades
D) Data Drift is a synonym for judge LLM hallucination
explanation: Data Drift is specifically about the WORLD changing, not your system or model changing: if your golden dataset says 'the correct answer to X is Y' because that was true when the golden was written, but the underlying business fact (a price, a policy, a course curriculum) has since changed, that golden is now silently WRONG -- your app could give the new, correct answer and get penalized by an outdated ground truth, or give the old, drifted answer and get incorrectly rewarded. This is precisely why golden datasets need periodic refresh cycles as a distinct discipline from regression testing (which assumes your ground truth is still valid and just checks your system against it) -- regression testing alone can't catch a golden dataset that's become stale due to the world moving on. A, C, and D each misdefine the concept.

question: The Self-Improving Loop (production failure -> added to offline golden dataset -> retest -> redeploy) is framed as something worth NAMING explicitly in an interview, even if you're already doing it informally. Why?
options: A) Naming it has no practical value; it's purely a marketing term

B) Explicitly naming an existing practice (e.g. a two-tier CI strategy already folding production failures back into goldens) reframes it as a deliberate architecture decision rather than a reactive, ad hoc fix -- signaling intentional system design rather than fire-fighting
C) The loop must be renamed before it can be implemented in DeepEval
D) It only applies to safety-related production failures, not quality failures
explanation: This connects directly to the theory addendum's broader thesis: general LLM-eval vocabulary sits ABOVE DeepEval mechanics, and using it deliberately frames tool-specific answers as coming from a coherent evaluation strategy rather than isolated tool knowledge. If you're already doing something like folding production failures back into your golden dataset as part of a two-tier CI strategy, explicitly calling that 'the Self-Improving Loop' in an interview signals you understand it as a deliberate architectural pattern with a name and a rationale -- versus describing the same behavior as 'yeah, we just add failing cases when we find them,' which reads as reactive improvisation even if the underlying practice is identical. C and D invent false constraints; A dismisses real communicative value in precise, deliberate vocabulary.

question: Which is the correct 'Top 3 to actually rehearse' list from the Theory Addendum, and what do they have in common as interview answers?
options: A) RAG Triad, Plan Quality vs Adherence, Tool Correctness vs Argument Correctness -- all DeepEval-mechanics soundbites

B) The Interaction Trap (concrete workflow-level failure example), MAE for judge calibration (named, quantified answer), Captured vs Computed signals (precise production-monitoring vocabulary) -- all are named, specific, rehearsed answers that beat vague generic responses to common interview questions
C) Model Evals vs Application Evals, the 3 Risk Pillars, the 5 Human Eval styles -- purely definitional recall
D) Data Drift, Stratified Sampling, the Self-Improving Loop -- all about production cost control specifically
explanation: The addendum explicitly flags these 3 as the highest-priority items to rehearse, out of everything covered: 1) The Interaction Trap -- a concrete, memorable workflow-level failure example (retriever partial-fail + generator mis-pick) that answers a very likely interview question directly. 2) MAE for judge calibration -- a named, quantified metric that beats a vague 'we compare to humans' answer. 3) Captured vs Computed signals -- precise vocabulary for how production monitoring actually works, beating a hand-wavy description. What unifies all 3 is that they're SPECIFIC, NAMED answers to commonly-asked questions, which read as far more credible than generic responses -- that's the actual selection criterion, not topic area. A, C, and D each pick a different (also valid, but not the documented Top-3) grouping.

question: The 'White-Box vs Black-Box' framing is called a key Director-level talking point. What's the core claim, and what does it imply about testing organization?
options: A) Agentic metrics are black-box -- deepeval never needs access to your code

B) Agentic metrics are white-box, not black-box -- @observe must be added to the DEV's own code (agent orchestrator, tool wrappers, LLM call sites); this means AI test strategy requires embedding testers into the dev workflow EARLY, not testing after the fact, and someone must own the convention for which functions get type="agent" vs "tool" vs "llm"
C) White-box framing only applies to safety metrics, not agentic ones
D) White-box testing means using a different, non-LLM judge model
explanation: This is a deliberate, high-leverage interview talking point for a leadership-level role: unlike black-box UI automation (e.g. Selenium/Playwright testing a deployed app from the outside with no code access), agentic evaluation with deepeval fundamentally requires @observe decoration INSIDE the developer's own code -- the orchestrator, the tool wrapper functions, the LLM call sites. That's white-box by necessity. The organizational implication is significant: you can't bolt AI testing on after the fact the way you might with UI automation; testers/QA need to be embedded into the dev workflow from early on, and someone needs to own the convention for span typing (agent/tool/llm) across the team so tracing stays consistent and useful. This is explicitly framed as a natural bridge from a Selenium/Playwright background, since white-box vs black-box instrumentation is a distinction that background already reasons about daily.

question: Per the documented 'Priority Summary' pacing for an interview, which RAG metric is explicitly called out as the one gap even within an otherwise 'full confidence, all hands-on' RAG story?
